title: Float equality compared with == instead of math.isclose(), causing false negatives due to floating-point precision.

root_cause.title: Float equality compared with == instead of math.isclose(), causing false negatives due to floating-point precision.
root_cause.pattern: A float value is compared using == (or !=) directly against another float or a float literal, rather than using math.isclose() or an absolute-tolerance check.

twins.reasoning: Arithmetic result of a subtraction of two floats is compared with == against a third float; rounding in the subtraction can produce a value that is not bit-for-bit equal to expected_saving.
A float is compared directly with the literal 0.0; any tiny residual from upstream arithmetic will make the comparison return False even for logically-zero prices.
Two float discount rates are compared with ==; the same IEEE-754 precision issue that existed in pricing.py applies here.
Invoice total (likely accumulated from line items) compared with == against an expected float; classic accumulation error.
Paid and owed amounts are floats that may have been computed via arithmetic; direct == comparison is unreliable.
Tax values involve multiplication (rate * amount) which introduces floating-point error; == comparison will silently mis-classify correct tax computations.

variants.description: Use 'not (total != expected)' instead of == to compare two floats — logically equivalent but still relies on != for floats.
Introduce a brand-new module src/refunds.py with 'return refunded == original' — same mistake in a previously clean file.
Store the arithmetic result in a local variable 'difference = paid - owed' then compare 'difference == 0.0' — the == is one step removed from the call site.
Use 'abs(computed_tax - expected_tax) == 0' — looks like a tolerance check but uses == 0 with no epsilon, reproducing the same precision failure.
Compare a float to the integer literal 0 instead of 0.0: 'return price == 0' — same mistake, different literal type.
Introduce a private helper '_floats_equal(a, b): return a == b' and call it — the bug is hidden one call-level deeper.
